title: One cell, then two: how you grew and how your body stays new

summary.text: You started as one cell, smaller than the dot of a pencil. Today you are made of about 30 to 40 trillion cells. No one added them from outside. Each cell copied the instructions inside her, and then split in two. The same copying goes on today. The lining of your gut is replaced in days, and your skin in weeks. In this unit you cut the tip off a young root to find where plants really grow, and you work out how a body can be rebuilt all the time and still be yours.
summary.art: A single round cell on the left, then arrows doubling it into 2, 4 and 8 cells, ending in a small child standing on the right.

intro.hook: Look at a young root of a moong sprout, about one finger-joint long. Tomorrow it will be much longer. Where does the new length come from? Does the whole root stretch like a rubber band, or does the root grow in one small place?
intro.text: Think about your own skin as well. Every day, some of it rubs off on your clothes and in the bath. Yet your skin never wears thin. Something is making new skin as fast as the old skin leaves. In this unit you find out where new cells come from, how one cell becomes two, and how that made you.
intro.art: A moong sprout with a short white root on a damp plate beside a ruler, and a child's finger pointing at the root's pale tip.

outcomes: I can say that a cell makes a new cell by copying her instructions and splitting into two, and that this is how living things grow and mend.
I can describe the order of cell division: copy the instructions, line up the copies, pull them apart, and pinch (or wall) the cell in two.
I can use a fair test to show that a root grows at its tip, where cells divide, and explain what the result means.
I can explain how one fertilised egg became a whole body, and why a skin cell and a muscle cell can come from the same first cell.
I can give examples of cells that are replaced in days, weeks or months, and cells that last for most of a life.
I can work out how many cells there are after a number of doublings, and say why doubling grows so fast.
I can explain why a body is not the same stuff for ever, and give two views on what stays the same.

terms.meaning: The way one cell becomes two. The cell copies her instructions, shares the copies out, and splits.
terms.example: A root grows longer because cells at the tip keep dividing.
terms.art: One round cell pinching in the middle into two round cells.

terms.meaning: The two new cells made when one cell divides. The word daughter is used for both, whatever the sex of the body.
terms.example: One skin cell divides and makes two daughter skin cells.
terms.art: One large cell and two smaller cells beside it joined by arrows labelled daughter cells.

terms.meaning: The long instruction book inside a cell. It is written in four letters, A, T, C and G. It is copied each time the cell divides.
terms.example: A human cell holds about 6 billion DNA letters. Written out, they would fill thousands of thick books.
terms.art: A twisting ladder with rungs in four colours, labelled DNA.

terms.meaning: One long piece of DNA wound up tightly, like a thread on a reel. Chromosomes become easy to see when a cell is about to divide.
terms.example: A human cell has 46 chromosomes, which is 23 pairs.
terms.art: Forty-six short thick threads arranged in pairs inside a round cell.

terms.meaning: One short stretch of DNA with the instructions for making one useful thing, such as a part of the body's machinery.
terms.example: One gene carries the instructions for the red substance that carries oxygen in blood.
terms.art: A long DNA thread with one short section lit up and labelled gene.

terms.meaning: The way a cell that has a nucleus gives each daughter cell one full set of chromosomes. The name comes from a Greek word for thread.
terms.example: Mitosis happens when a skin cell, a root-tip cell or a gut-lining cell divides.
terms.art: Four small drawings in a row showing chromosomes copying, lining up, pulling apart and splitting.

terms.meaning: The repeating life of a dividing cell: grow, copy the instructions, check the copies, divide, and start again.
terms.example: A cell in a root tip may go once round the cycle in about a day.
terms.art: A circle with four arrows labelled grow, copy, check and divide.

terms.meaning: The first cell of a new person or other animal. She forms when a sperm cell joins an egg cell, and she divides to make the whole body.
terms.example: Every person began as a fertilised egg about the size of a full stop.
terms.art: A tiny round cell beside a full stop, with a ruler showing it is about a tenth of a millimetre.

terms.meaning: A very young body that has just started to divide. It is made of only a few cells, or a few thousand.
terms.example: After three rounds of division, an embryo has 8 cells.
terms.art: A cluster of 8 round cells like a tiny bunch of grapes.

terms.meaning: A cell that has taken on one job, such as carrying oxygen or making a muscle pull. She uses only the pages of the instruction book that job needs.
terms.example: A muscle cell and a skin cell hold the same instructions but use different pages.
terms.art: A long thin muscle cell and a flat skin cell side by side, with the same book icon inside each.

terms.meaning: A cell that can keep dividing, and can make daughter cells that become specialised for different jobs.
terms.example: Stem cells in your bone marrow make new blood cells every second.
terms.art: A round stem cell at the centre with arrows to three different shaped cells.

terms.meaning: The growing region of a plant, such as the tip of a root or a shoot, where cells divide again and again.
terms.example: The pale tip of a moong root is a meristem.
terms.art: A root tip drawn in section with the small dividing cells at the very end highlighted.

terms.meaning: The way a bacterium divides. She copies her one loop of DNA, grows longer, and pinches in the middle into two.
terms.example: A bacterium in warm milk can divide every 20 to 30 minutes.
terms.art: A rod-shaped bacterium stretching and pinching into two rods.

terms.meaning: The way a yeast cell often divides. A small bump grows on the side of the cell, takes a copy of the instructions, and breaks off.
terms.example: Yeast cells in dough make buds.
terms.art: A round yeast cell with a smaller bud growing on one side.

terms.meaning: Making new cells to take the place of old ones that have worn out or died. Scientists also call this cell turnover.
terms.example: The lining of your gut is replaced every few days.
terms.art: A row of old cells flaking away on top and new cells pushing up from below.

terms.meaning: How a body repairs a cut. Cells near the edges divide and move in, until the gap is closed.
terms.example: A scrape on a knee is usually closed in a week or two.
terms.art: A cut in skin shown in three stages as new cells fill the gap.

explanations.concept: A cell makes a new cell by splitting in two
explanations.description: Every cell comes from a cell that was there before. A cell cannot be made from nothing, and she cannot be sewn together from parts. She has to divide. One cell becomes two, two become four, and four become eight. That is how a seed grows into a plant and an egg grows into an animal, including a human. It is also how a cut heals. A cell that divides does not die and leave a body behind. She becomes the two daughters.
examples: A bacterium in warm milk divides into two, then four, then eight.
A yeast cell grows a bud and the bud breaks off as a new cell.
A fertilised egg divides into 2 cells, then 4, then 8.
explanations.art: A single cell becoming two, then four, then eight, drawn as a family tree that grows downward.
explanations.definition: Cell division is when one cell copies her instructions and then splits into two daughter cells, each with a full set of the instructions.

explanations.description: DNA looks like a twisted ladder. Each rung joins two letters. A joins only with T, and C joins only with G. So each side of the ladder spells out the other. To copy it, the cell unzips the ladder down the middle. Then she builds a new matching side on each half. The result is two complete ladders, each with one old side and one new side. A human cell copies about 6 billion letters in a few hours, and only a handful of mistakes get through.
examples: Unzip a zip fastener, and each half can be matched with a new half.
A line of letters ATTC pairs with TAAG on the other side.
Each new DNA ladder has one old side and one new side.
explanations.art: A twisted DNA ladder unzipping down the middle, with new matching pieces joining each half to make two full ladders.
explanations.definition: DNA is the long molecule inside a cell that holds her instructions. Before a cell divides, she copies all of it.

explanations.concept: Chromosomes: the instruction book in 46 volumes
explanations.description: DNA is so long that it would not fit in the cell if it were loose. So it is wound up, like thread on a reel. Just before a cell divides, each chromosome has been copied, and the two copies stay joined in the middle so they look like an X. You get 23 chromosomes from your mother's egg and 23 from your father's sperm. Other living things have other numbers. A rice plant has 24, a dog has 78, and the Indian muntjac deer has just 6 in a female and 7 in a male.
examples: A fruit fly has 8 chromosomes, a chimpanzee has 48, and a human has 46.
The Indian muntjac, a small deer of Indian forests, has the fewest known of any mammal.
More chromosomes does not mean a cleverer or bigger living being.
explanations.art: A cell with 46 chromosomes in pairs, and a few animals shown beside the number of chromosomes each has.
explanations.definition: A chromosome is one long piece of DNA wound tightly around proteins. Humans have 46 chromosomes in most cells, which is 23 pairs.

explanations.description: After the copying, the cell goes through four steps. First, the chromosomes wind up tight and the nucleus wall breaks down. Second, the chromosomes line up across the middle of the cell. Third, thin threads called spindle fibres pull each pair apart, so one copy goes to each end. Fourth, the cell pinches in the middle, and two new nuclei form. The pulling is the important part. If one daughter got two copies and the other got none, the daughters would not work properly.
examples: It is like tugging a rope from both ends until it comes apart in the middle.
A dividing cell in an onion root tip shows the chromosomes lined up like a row of beads.
Mistakes in sharing are the cause of some illnesses that a person is born with.
explanations.art: Four drawings in a row: chromosomes winding tight, lining up in the middle, being pulled apart by threads, and the cell pinching into two.
explanations.definition: Mitosis is how a cell with a nucleus shares her copied chromosomes so that each daughter cell gets exactly one full set.

explanations.concept: How plant cells and animal cells finish dividing
explanations.description: An animal cell has a soft skin and no wall, so she can squeeze in around the middle, like a balloon pinched by a thread. A plant cell has a stiff wall outside the skin, so pinching is not possible. Instead, she builds a new wall from the middle outwards. The new wall is called a cell plate. This is part of why plants are stiff and why plant cells in a leaf look like boxes stacked neatly side by side.
examples: An animal cell pinches like a water balloon squeezed in the middle.
A plant cell builds a dividing wall, like putting up a partition in a room.
Bacteria also pinch in two, but they do not use mitosis.
explanations.art: An animal cell pinching in two beside a plant cell building a new wall across her middle.
explanations.definition: An animal cell finishes by pinching in the middle. A plant cell finishes by building a new wall across the middle.

explanations.concept: Why a root grows only at the tip
explanations.description: A few millimetres behind the tip, the cells of a root have stopped dividing. They are finished, and they only soak up water. So if you mark dots along a growing root, only the dots close to the tip move apart. The tip also has a thin cap that rubs through the soil and wears away, and it is replaced all the time. If you cut off the tip, the root usually stops lengthening. A root pushes down through the soil, but only the very end is doing the growing.
examples: A moong sprout's root grows about a centimetre in a day, almost all of it at the tip.
The stems of tulsi and chilli grow at shoot tips. Pinch the tip and the plant grows side branches instead.
A banyan's hanging roots grow downward until their tips reach the soil.
explanations.art: A root drawn in four zones: a cap at the very end, a dividing zone, a stretching zone, and an older zone with root hairs.
explanations.definition: A root grows longer at its tip. Cells divide in a small zone at the very end, and the new cells stretch a little just behind it.

explanations.concept: From one cell to you: a fertilised egg divides
explanations.description: The fertilised egg divides for the first time after about a day. Then 2 become 4, 4 become 8, and 8 become 16. After a few days the group is a hollow ball of cells. Over the weeks that follow the cells move, fold and take on different jobs. A baby is born after about nine months. A grown person has about 30 to 40 trillion cells. To reach that number from one cell takes at least 45 rounds of doubling, since 2 multiplied by itself 45 times is about 35 trillion. In real bodies it takes many more divisions than that, because cells also die and are replaced along the way.
examples: Identical twins form when the early group of cells splits into two groups, and each group makes a baby.
Doubling 10 times gives 1,024 cells. Doubling 20 times gives over a million.
A grown person is bigger than a baby mostly because they have more cells, not bigger cells.
explanations.art: A fertilised egg dividing into 2, 4, 8 and a hollow ball of cells, then a baby, with the number of doublings written under each.
explanations.definition: A new person starts as a fertilised egg, one cell. She divides many times, and the daughter cells take on different jobs.

explanations.concept: Same instructions, different jobs: specialised cells
explanations.description: A skin cell and a muscle cell are very different shapes. Yet each holds the same 46 chromosomes. They look different because they use different pages of the instruction book. A muscle cell uses pages that build the stretchy threads for pulling. A skin cell uses pages that build a tough, waterproof layer. Signals from the cells around her decide which pages a cell uses. In 1962 John Gurdon put the nucleus of a frog's gut cell into an egg whose own nucleus had been removed. The egg grew into a tadpole. So the gut cell had kept the whole book.
examples: A red blood cell loses her nucleus when she is made, and so can never divide.
A neuron is long and thin and sends signals, though she has the same instructions as a bone cell.
A cut piece of a tulsi stem can grow roots and become a whole new plant, since the cells still hold the whole book.
explanations.art: One book icon in the middle with arrows to a long muscle cell, a flat skin cell and a branching nerve cell, each with a different page highlighted.
explanations.definition: Specialised cells use different parts of the same instructions. Nearly every cell in your body holds the full set.

explanations.concept: Replacement: cells wear out and are rebuilt
explanations.description: Cells have different lifetimes. The lining of your gut is replaced in about 3 to 5 days, because food scrapes it all the time. The outer layer of skin is replaced in about a month. Red blood cells last about 4 months. A strand of hair stays for years. A few kinds are almost never replaced in a grown person. Most nerve cells in the thinking part of the brain and the cells in the lens of the eye are as old as you are, and heart muscle cells are replaced very slowly. The parts of the body that meet the world, like skin and the gut lining, are often replaced fastest. Scientists can tell how old a cell is. The bomb tests of the 1950s and 1960s put a kind of carbon called carbon-14 into the air. It went from the air into food, and from food into the DNA that was built when each cell was made.
examples: Dust and flakes in a sunbeam include tiny pieces of dead skin.
Your red blood cells are made at a rate of about two million every second, in the soft middle of your bones, called marrow.
A scar remains after a deep cut because the repair is done with tough fibres, not new skin.
explanations.art: A body outline with labels showing how long different parts last: gut lining days, skin weeks, blood months, fat and bone years, nerve cells a lifetime.
explanations.definition: Most cells wear out. New cells from dividing stem cells take the place of the old ones.

explanations.concept: What happens when cells divide too much
explanations.description: Cells do not divide all the time. They divide only when signals say so, and they stop when a gap is filled or when the copy has an error. Cancer begins when a cell gets damage in the instructions that control these signals. Then she divides again and again, and her daughters do too. The cluster can crowd out the cells next to it. Doctors can often treat cancer, especially when it is found early. A healthy body gets rid of most damaged cells before they cause trouble. Understanding how division is controlled is one of the biggest areas of research in medicine.
examples: A body's cells stop dividing when a cut has closed.
Smoke and strong sunlight can damage the instructions in cells they touch.
Finding a lump early gives doctors more ways to help.
explanations.art: A normal cell with a stop sign beside a damaged cell with the stop sign missing, and a growing cluster of cells.
explanations.definition: Cancer is a disease in which some cells in a body ignore the stop signals and divide when they should not.

explanations.concept: How many times can a cell divide?
explanations.description: In 1961 Leonard Hayflick found that human cells in a dish do not divide for ever. The ends of chromosomes, called telomeres, get a little shorter each time the DNA is copied. When they are short enough, the cell stops dividing. Some cells, such as stem cells and cancer cells, switch on a repair machine called telomerase that rebuilds the ends. Whether the shortening is a main cause of ageing in a whole body, or only one part of it, is still argued about.
examples: HeLa cells, taken from a cancer in 1951, keep dividing in dishes in labs all over the world.
Hydra, a tiny freshwater animal, seems to renew her cells without any sign of ageing.
A cell in a dish is in a very different place from a cell inside a body.
explanations.art: Chromosomes with caps at their ends, and the caps getting shorter after each of several divisions.

perspectives.explanation: Short telomeres make cells stop dividing, and this limit protects the body from cells that divide too much. It is one cause of ageing.
Telomeres matter, but a body ages for many reasons together, such as damage to proteins and to DNA. Telomere length alone does not predict how long a person lives.
Nobody yet knows how much of ageing comes from the limit on division. Studies in animals and in people keep giving mixed results.

explanations.definition: Most normal human cells, grown in a dish, divide about 40 to 60 times and then stop. This is called the Hayflick limit.

agreed.text: Every cell comes from another cell that divided.
agreed.evidence: Cells have been watched dividing under microscopes since the 1800s. No one has ever seen a cell form from non-living material in a lab or a body.

agreed.text: Before a cell divides, she copies all her DNA, and each daughter cell gets one full copy.
agreed.evidence: In 1958 Matthew Meselson and Franklin Stahl used heavy nitrogen to label DNA. After one round of copying, each new DNA held one old side and one new side.

agreed.text: Humans have 46 chromosomes in most body cells.
agreed.evidence: In 1956 Joe Hin Tjio and Albert Levan counted 46 in cells from the lungs of a human embryo. Counts of cells from many other people have given 46 since.

agreed.text: Nearly every cell in a body holds the same DNA, and specialised cells use different parts of it.
agreed.evidence: In 1962 John Gurdon grew tadpoles from eggs given the nucleus of a gut cell. In 1996 a sheep, Dolly, was cloned from a cell taken from an adult sheep's udder.

agreed.text: Many kinds of cell in the body are replaced throughout life, but some are not.
agreed.evidence: From 2005 on, teams led by Jonas Frisén, including Kirsten Spalding, Olaf Bergmann and Ratan Bhardwaj, used the carbon-14 left in the air by bomb tests to date human cells. About a tenth of fat cells were renewed each year. Heart muscle cells were renewed very slowly. Nerve cells in the thinking part of the brain were as old as the person.

agreed.text: Cell division in bacteria, yeast, plants and animals follows the same basic pattern: copy the instructions, share the copies, and split.
agreed.evidence: The same kinds of molecules do the copying in all of them. Genes for the copying machinery are so alike that a human gene can sometimes work in a yeast cell.

challenging.claim: Every cell in your body is replaced every seven years.
challenging.for: Some cells really are replaced in days or weeks, so people guess that the whole body is renewed in a fixed time.
challenging.against: Different cells have very different lifetimes. Cells in the gut last days, but most cells in the thinking part of the brain and in the eye lens stay for life. There is no single number of years for the whole body.

challenging.claim: Once you are grown, your body stops making new cells.
challenging.who: Many people, and some old textbooks.
challenging.for: A grown person does not get taller, so it seems that growing has stopped.
challenging.against: A grown body makes millions of new cells every second, in the marrow, skin and gut. What stops is growing bigger, and not the making of cells.

challenging.claim: Adult humans can grow new brain cells in the memory area of the brain.
challenging.who: Some neuroscientists say this, and others disagree.
challenging.for: In 2018 Maura Boldrini and colleagues found signs of young neurons in the memory area (the hippocampus) of people up to the age of 79.
challenging.against: Also in 2018, Shawn Sorrells and colleagues found almost none in people past childhood. The two groups used different ways of preserving and testing brains.

challenging.claim: Cells in a body are all copies, so there are no differences between them.
challenging.for: All the cells start from one fertilised egg and share the same DNA.
challenging.against: The DNA is nearly the same, but cells use different parts of it, and so they look and work very differently. A few mistakes also creep in during copying, so older bodies carry small differences between their cells.

challenging.claim: A root stretches along its whole length as it grows.
challenging.who: Many children and adults, before they test it.
challenging.for: A root clearly gets longer, and it seems natural that every part grows a little.
challenging.against: Dots marked along a growing root show that only the part within a few millimetres of the tip lengthens. The rest stays the same length.

big_questions.q: A cell that divides turns into two cells. Did the first cell die, or did she become two?
big_questions.hint: Think about what is left behind after a bacterium divides, compared with a person who dies.

big_questions.q: Your skin cells are replaced every few weeks. In what way is it still your skin?
big_questions.hint: Think about a school uniform that gets patched, or a river whose water changes.

big_questions.q: Two cells with exactly the same instructions can grow into a muscle and a skin cell. What decides which one each becomes?
big_questions.hint: Think about a book where each reader only turns to some pages.

big_questions.q: Your body is a community of about 30 to 40 trillion cells. Most of them obey the signals that tell them when to stop dividing. Who is in charge?
big_questions.hint: Think about a city, and about whether any single person runs it.

big_questions.q: Cancer cells in a dish can divide for ever, but normal cells stop. Is a cell that never stops dividing a winner or a problem?
big_questions.hint: Think about what the rest of the body needs from each cell.

big_questions.q: Some cells in a body are as old as you are, and some are a few days old. Which are the real you?
big_questions.hint: Think about whether the answer could be the pattern, and not the pieces.

big_questions.q: Henrietta Lacks's cells were taken in 1951 without anyone asking her. They have helped medicine for 70 years. Who should decide what happens to cells from a body?
big_questions.hint: Think about what she would have chosen, and what her family would say now.

big_questions.q: A bacterium divides every 20 minutes and a nerve cell may never divide. Is one way of living better?
big_questions.hint: Think about what each kind of cell does for the living being she belongs to.

story.title: The Root That Would Not Be Pulled
story.note: A made-up story with real science and a real tradition. In Meghalaya, the Khasi and Jaintia peoples guide the roots of the rubber fig (Ficus elastica) across streams to make living bridges. A bridge takes many years to become strong enough to walk on. The characters and their names are imagined.
text: Daiaphi lived in a village above a deep green valley in Meghalaya, where it rains for most of the year. When she was six, her grandmother had taken her to a stream at the bottom of the valley. A bridge crossed it, made of living roots, as thick as a man's arm. They twisted across the water like a long green rope, and children and goats walked over it every day.
'Who built it?' Daiaphi had asked.
'My grandfather's grandfather started it,' said her grandmother. 'He never walked on it. His grandchildren did. We keep it growing now.'

Now Daiaphi was ten, and in Class 5. Her family was growing a new bridge, further down the same stream. It was her job to look after a young root from a rubber fig tree on the bank. For six years she had guided it. The root crept out of the tree, passed through a hollow trunk of an areca palm, and was now halfway across the stream. It was thin, and a little pale at the end, and it grew toward the far bank only a hand's width each month.

One morning a man came from the town, with a clipboard and a coil of strong rope. His name was Mr Rynjah. He was an engineer, and he was kind, but he was in a hurry. A road was being built, and the officials wanted to know whether the new bridge could be ready in two years.
'Two years?' said Daiaphi's father. 'It will be fifteen.'
'We can speed it up,' said Mr Rynjah. 'Tie a rope to the root's end and pull it across. A little each day. Roots stretch, don't they? The whole root will lengthen, and the gap will close.'

Daiaphi's father looked at the root, and he looked at the rope, and he looked uncertain. Maybe Mr Rynjah was right. He had studied in the town. Daiaphi's grandmother only shook her head slowly and said nothing.

Daiaphi had a school notebook with her. In Class 4, her teacher, Madam Lyngdoh, had shown the class how to put tiny dots of ink on a sprout's root, and how to measure them again after a day. Daiaphi had done it with a bean. She still remembered what the dots had shown. She took a deep breath.
'Please, may I try something first?' she said. 'It will take only two days.'
Mr Rynjah looked at his watch. But her father nodded.

Daiaphi found a thin black thread. With her grandmother's help, she tied small knots of thread around the young root, every two fingers' width, from the pale tip back toward the tree, six knots in all. She drew them in her notebook. Then she wrote the distance between each knot.

Two days later, the whole village came to look, because by now everybody was curious. Daiaphi measured the knots again. The gaps between the old knots, near the tree, were exactly as wide as before. They had not grown by even a hair. Only the last gap, between the knot closest to the tip and the tip itself, had grown longer. It had grown by almost a finger's width.

'Look,' said Daiaphi. 'The root is not stretching along its length. It only grows at the end. The long part behind is finished. It has become strong and thick. The new part is only at the very tip, where the cells keep splitting in two.'
'Cells?' said Mr Rynjah slowly.

'Tiny rooms that everything is made of,' she said. 'Our teacher told us. At the tip they copy themselves and split, again and again, and then the new ones stretch a little. Behind the tip they stop. So if you pull the root, you cannot make the thick part longer. You will only tear the tip. And if the tip is gone, the root cannot grow at all.'
Nobody spoke. A drop fell from a leaf.

Then Mr Rynjah crouched down beside the stream and looked for a long time at the thin pale end of the root. He took a pencil and wrote something on his clipboard. After a while he said, 'So the only way to make it faster is to protect that small tip and keep it wet and well fed.'
'And to wait,' said Daiaphi's grandmother, and she smiled for the first time that morning.
'Fifteen years,' said Mr Rynjah. He laughed. 'The officials will not like it. But they will like a bridge that falls into the stream even less.'

He did not take the rope. Instead he asked the village to show him how they guided the tip with a hollow areca trunk, and he sent a note to the officials that said the new bridge should be opened when it was ready, and not before.

That evening Daiaphi sat by the stream with her grandmother. The old bridge hummed in the wind. 'Its oldest roots,' said her grandmother, 'were made before my own grandmother was born. And at the very ends, there are still tiny new tips, growing today.'
'So the bridge is old and new at the same time,' said Daiaphi.

'Like a person,' said her grandmother. 'Like you, with your scraped knees mending.' She touched Daiaphi's hand. 'Every part of us is being made again, at the edges, all the time. And still we say, this is my granddaughter.'

Daiaphi looked down at the thin pale tip of her own young root, hanging over the water. It was so small. But in it, every hour, cells were splitting in two, and the bridge for her own grandchildren was a little closer.
story.epiphany: A root does not stretch along its length. It grows only at the tip, where cells copy themselves and split in two.
ask: Why would pulling the root with a rope have torn it instead of lengthening it?
If the thread knots stayed the same distance apart, what does that say about the part of the root behind the tip?
Daiaphi's grandmother said that we are made again at the edges, all the time. Where on your body might that be true?
