roots.context: In Cut the Tip, the roots with their tips cut off hardly grew, because a root grows at the tip, where cells divide. Now we ask what it means that a body is rebuilt all the time, and what stays the same when the cells change.

deep_truth.truth: Often, the parts of you that meet the world are rebuilt fastest. Your gut lining is replaced in days and your skin in weeks, but cells that are protected deep inside can last for years. A living body is not a finished thing that gets mended now and then. It is made new, all the time, wherever it touches the world.
deep_truth.habit: We picture a body as a finished object that stays the same, and that is only mended when it is hurt. Cells show that rebuilding is the normal state, and that the busiest rebuilding happens at the edges.
deep_truth.evidence: In Cut the Tip, the roots whose tips were cut off hardly grew. In Dots on a Root, the finished part behind the tip did not lengthen. Skin flakes, gut lining and the root cap are all replaced often, while the cells in the eye lens stay for life.

three.who_am_i: You are not a thing that stays still. Parts of you are new every day, and parts of you are older than any of your birthdays.
three.what_is_life: A living being keeps copying her cells so that she can keep going. Life is a process of making and remaking, and not a block of stuff.
three.what_is_this_world: The atoms in a new skin cell came from food, water and air, and a few weeks later they go back to the world as flakes. The world flows through every body.

roots.thread: A fertilised egg has no skin, no gut, no blood and no bones. All of them come from one cell that copied her instructions and divided. The atoms in each new cell come from the food you ate, and the food came from plants, soil, rain and sunlight. When old cells wear out, their atoms go back to the world, and may be in the next plant, the next bird, the next child. So a body is made of stuff from the world that stays for a while, arranged by instructions that are copied from cell to cell. One cell becomes many cells, again and again.

teachings.teaching: Uddalaka teaches his son Shvetaketu about a great tree. If the life leaves one branch, that branch dries up. If it leaves the whole tree, the whole tree dries up. The same life is in all of it.
teachings.link: A root grows only at the tip, but the tip is fed by the whole tree. The living part and the finished part are one tree.

teachings.teaching: Plutarch tells how the Athenians kept the ship of Theseus for hundreds of years. As planks rotted, they replaced them with new wood. Thinkers argued about whether it was still the same ship.
teachings.link: Your skin and gut lining are replaced like planks. The old puzzle becomes a question about your own body.

teachings.teaching: A person is born soft and flexible, and at death is hard and stiff. Green plants are soft and full of sap, and when dead they are dry and brittle. The soft and yielding belongs to life.
teachings.link: The root tip is the softest, palest, wettest part of the plant. That is also the part that grows.

science.text: Rudolf Schoenheimer used heavy forms of hydrogen and nitrogen in the 1930s to follow molecules in the body. He showed that fats and proteins in a body are broken down and rebuilt all the time, even in a body that stays the same weight.
Whether adult humans make new nerve cells in the memory area of the brain is still argued about. Two groups looked in 2018 and found different answers.

other_view.view: He argued that the sense of being one fixed self is a story the brain tells, and not a thing hidden inside. If he is right, there is no hidden self to look for. There is only the changing pattern of the body and the story the brain tells.

practice.title: Looking at your own hand
practice.say: Hold one hand in front of you and look at it slowly. Breathe in and out three times. Remember that the top skin you see is made of cells that have finished their work. Underneath, new cells are pushing up. In about a month, this skin will be new. Ask yourself quietly, which part of me is this hand?
practice.kid: Look at your hand. Breathe in and out three times. The skin on top is old and the skin underneath is new. In a month, it will all be new. Which part is you?

ask: If every plank of a ship is replaced one at a time, is it the same ship? Is your body the same body?
What would you want to stay the same about you, if every cell in your skin and gut were replaced?
What makes you you: the pattern of your body, or the instructions copied into your cells?
roots.art: A child's hand held open, with thin golden threads running from the skin into a plant, a bowl of food and the soil, and flakes drifting away from the surface.

games.title: Days, Weeks or Years? The Replacement Race
games.context: This is a guessing game about how fast the cells of your body, and some other living cells, are replaced. Each card names a kind of cell. You guess how long it lasts or how often it divides.

setup.art: Twenty cards in a shuffled pile in the middle of a table, with four time tokens in front of each player.
setup.caption: 1. Cut out the cards and the tokens. Shuffle the cards into a pile.

setup.art: A reader holding up a card, while two other players each put a token face down in front of them.
setup.caption: 2. The reader reads a card. Everyone else picks a token and puts it face down.

setup.art: The tokens turned over together, and the reader turning the card over to show the answer.
setup.caption: 3. Turn the tokens over. The reader shows the back of the card.

printables.title: 20 two-sided cards: a kind of cell on the front, and how long it lasts or how often it divides on the back

items.f: Curd bacteria in warm milk. How long between one division and the next?
items.b: HOURS. In warm milk a curd bacterium can divide in under an hour. That is why one spoon of curd can set a whole pot overnight.

items.f: A yeast cell in warm dough with sugar. How long before she grows a bud?
items.b: HOURS. A yeast cell can grow and release a bud in about an hour and a half when she is warm and has sugar.

items.f: A gut bacterium called E. coli in a warm place with food. How long between divisions?
items.b: HOURS. Under the best conditions, one E. coli divides about every 20 minutes. Most of the E. coli in a body are harmless.

items.f: The cells lining your small gut, which food scrapes all day.
items.b: DAYS. The lining of the gut is replaced about every 3 to 5 days. Stem cells deep in tiny pits keep making new ones.

items.f: The lining of your stomach, which sits in strong acid.
items.b: DAYS. The stomach lining is replaced in a few days, so the acid does not wear a hole through it.

items.f: Taste cells on your tongue.
items.b: DAYS. A taste cell lasts about 10 days, and then a new one takes her place.

items.f: The cells on the inside of your cheek.
items.b: DAYS. Cheek-lining cells are replaced in about one to two weeks.

items.f: A neutrophil, a white blood cell that fights germs.
items.b: DAYS. Marrow makes huge numbers of neutrophils, and each one lasts only from several hours to a few days.

items.f: The clear front window of the eye, called the cornea. How long before the surface cells are new?
items.b: DAYS. The surface of the cornea is replaced in about a week, which is why small scratches often heal quickly.

items.f: The top layer of your skin.
items.b: WEEKS TO MONTHS. Skin cells take about a month to rise from the bottom of the top layer to the surface, where they flake off.

items.f: A red blood cell.
items.b: WEEKS TO MONTHS. A red blood cell lasts about 4 months. Marrow makes about two million new ones every second.

items.f: A fingernail, from the bottom edge to the free tip.
items.b: WEEKS TO MONTHS. A fingernail takes about 4 to 6 months to grow out from the base to the tip.

items.f: A scalp hair, from when it starts growing until it falls out.
items.b: A YEAR OR MORE. A scalp hair grows for about 2 to 6 years, then rests and falls out. A new hair starts in the same place.

items.f: A fat cell.
items.b: A YEAR OR MORE. Fat cells live about 10 years on average. A body can make them swell or shrink without changing their number much.

items.f: The bones of a grown-up's skeleton.
items.b: A YEAR OR MORE. Bone is taken apart and rebuilt in small patches, so a grown-up's skeleton is renewed about every 10 years.

items.f: Liver cells.
items.b: A YEAR OR MORE. A liver cell lasts about a year. A damaged liver can also regrow much of itself.

items.f: Muscle cells of the heart.
items.b: A YEAR OR MORE. Most heart muscle cells last a whole life. About 1 in 100 are replaced each year in a young adult, and fewer later.

items.f: Nerve cells in the thinking part of the brain, called the cortex.
items.b: A YEAR OR MORE. Almost all of them are as old as you are. They stop dividing around the time of birth.

items.f: Cells in the middle of the lens of the eye.
items.b: A YEAR OR MORE. The cells in the middle of the lens were made before you were born and are never replaced.

items.f: Sound-sensing hair cells in the inner ear.
items.b: A YEAR OR MORE. In people they are not replaced if they are lost, which is why loud noise can harm hearing for life. Birds regrow theirs, and scientists study how.

printables.title: 16 time tokens: four sets of four

rules: Hours means the cell divides again in less than a day. Days means the cell is replaced in two weeks or less. Weeks to months means up to about six months. A year or more means the cell lasts that long, or for life.
One player is the reader. The reader takes the top card and reads the front aloud. The reader does not show the back.
Every other player puts one time token face down. Then everyone turns the tokens over together.
The reader turns the card over and reads the back. Every player whose token matches the first words of the back scores one point.
The reader's job passes to the player on the left after every card. With two players, the parent and the child swap after every card. The reader never guesses on their own card.
Playing alone: put a token face down for each card, turn the card over, and score a point for each correct token. Try to beat your own score next time.
The game ends when all 20 cards have been read. The player with the most points wins. If there is a tie, the tied players share the win.

flow.do: Cut out the 20 cards and the 16 tokens. Shuffle the cards and make a pile. Give each player one token of each kind.
flow.say: These cards name a kind of cell. Each player gets four tokens. We will guess how long each kind lasts.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards and tokens. Shuffle the cards. Each player takes four tokens.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Replacement Race. You get the cards ready.

flow.do: Play the first six cards. After each one, read the back aloud. After card three, ask the question below.
flow.say: The reader reads the front. Everyone puts a token face down. Turn them over together. The reader reads the back. Who scored?
flow.kid: The reader reads a card. Pick a token. Turn it over. Check the back.

ask.q: What do the cells that are replaced fastest have in common?
good: Food or the air rubs them.
They are on the edges of the body.

flow.context: In this step, you play the first six cards.

flow.do: Play the next eight cards. Swap the reader's job after every card. Keep a tally of points on paper.
flow.say: Keep going. Think about this. Cells that wear out quickly are the ones that meet the world.
flow.kid: Play on. Cells that meet the world wear out fastest.
flow.think: Which cells on the cards were replaced fastest, and which slowest?
flow.context: In this step, you play eight more cards and start to see a pattern.

flow.do: Play the last six cards. Count the points. The player with the most points wins.
flow.say: Last six cards. Then we add up the points and talk about what we learned.
flow.kid: Play the last six cards. Add up your points.
flow.context: In this step, you play the last cards and add up the score.

flow.do: Lay the 20 cards in four rows by time: Hours, Days, Weeks to months, A year or more. Look at which cells are in the first rows. Then ask your child the questions below. Let them answer in their own words.
flow.say: Look at the cells that last the longest. Why might it be good for a brain cell to last all your life? And why might it be good for a gut cell to be replaced in days?
flow.kid: Which cells last the longest? Which are replaced fastest? Why?

ask.q: Why might a gut cell be replaced in days?
good: Food scrapes it and the acid wears it.

ask.q: Why might a brain cell last a lifetime?
good: A new cell would not have the old connections.
She is safe inside the skull.

flow.parent: A nerve cell is joined to thousands of others. If she were replaced, the new cell would have to learn every connection again. That is one idea about why nerve cells last. It is an idea, and scientists are still studying it.
flow.context: In this step, you talk about the pattern you found in the cards.

experiments.title: Cut the Tip: where does a root grow?
experiments.question: If you snip the tip off a young moong root, will the root still grow as much as a root with its tip left on?
experiments.predict: Before you cut anything, guess. Will the roots with the tip cut off grow more, the same, or less than the roots left alone? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Every root is from the same moong seeds, on the same kind of plate and tissue, in the same warm place. All roots are touched by the scissors in the same way. On plate A the scissors only touch the tip and cut nothing. On plate B the scissors cut off 3 millimetres of the tip. So the only difference is the missing tip, and any difference in growth comes from that. Plate A is the control.

materials.item: a small handful (about 15) of moong (green gram) seeds, soaked in the evening and sprouted in a damp cloth until the roots are 5 to 15 millimetres long (usually the next evening)
2 flat plates or steel katoris with flat bottoms
kitchen tissue or a clean cotton cloth, cut to fit the plates
a small pair of scissors (a grown-up cuts)
a ruler marked in millimetres, and a piece of thread for bending roots
a pen and sticky labels or paper marked A and B
a water spray bottle or a spoon for dripping water
a magnifying glass, if you have one
two lids or two upturned plates, to cover the plates

schedule.what: In the evening, soak the moong seeds for about 8 hours or overnight, then drain them and wrap them in a damp cloth.
Guess, set up two plates, measure every root and cut the tips on plate B.
Measure every root after one day.
Measure every root after two days, find the averages and explain what you saw.

experiments.safety: A grown-up does the cutting, because the scissors are sharp and the root is tiny. Wash hands after handling the sprouts. Do not eat sprouts that smell bad or have fuzzy patches.
experiments.record: Write the length of every root at the start, after one day and after two days. Work out how much each root grew. Find the average for plate A and for plate B. Draw a bar for each plate.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you find out where a root gets longer. You cut the tip off some roots and leave other roots alone, and then you measure both for two days.

setup.art: Moong seeds soaking in a bowl of water, then wrapped in a damp cloth in a steel container, with small white roots just showing.
setup.caption: 1. Soak moong seeds overnight. Then keep them in a damp cloth for a day, until roots show.

setup.art: Two plates labelled A and B, each with four sprouts lying on damp tissue, and a ruler measuring one root.
setup.caption: 2. Put four sprouts on each plate. Measure each root and write the length.

setup.art: A grown-up with small scissors cutting a tiny piece off the tip of one root on plate B, while on plate A the closed scissors only touch a tip.
setup.caption: 3. On plate B, snip 3 millimetres off each tip. On plate A, only touch the tips.

setup.art: Both plates covered with damp tissue and a lid, side by side in a warm cupboard.
setup.caption: 4. Cover both plates. Keep them together in a warm, dark place.

setup.art: A child measuring a root with a thread laid along it and then a ruler, with a table of numbers beside the plates.
setup.caption: 5. After one day and again after two days, measure every root.

flow.do: Soak a small handful (about 15) of moong seeds in water for about 8 hours or overnight. Drain them. Wrap them in a damp cloth in a bowl. Keep them somewhere warm.
flow.say: We will grow some moong sprouts first. Soak the seeds overnight. Tomorrow we wrap them in a damp cloth.
flow.kid: Soak the moong in water overnight. Drain them. Wrap them in a damp cloth.
flow.parent: You need roots between 5 and 15 millimetres. In a warm kitchen this usually takes about a day after soaking; in cool weather it can take two, so start earlier. Sprinkle the cloth with water twice a day. It should be damp, not dripping. Do not worry if a few seeds do not sprout: that is why you soak extra.
flow.context: This is the first step of Cut the Tip. You start the sprouts one day before the test.

flow.do: Look at the sprouts with your child. Find the root of each one. Ask for a guess and a reason, and write both down.
flow.say: Look at these roots. Tomorrow I will cut the tip off some of them. Do you think they will still grow longer? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Look at the roots. We will cut the tips off some. Will they still grow? Why?

ask.q: Which part of the root do you think grows longer?
good: All of it, like a rubber band.

ask.q: What do you think will happen to a root with no tip?

flow.parent: Do not correct a guess. Most children think the whole root stretches, and that is a good place to start. Write the guesses on the page with the table.
flow.wait: Wait until the roots are 5 to 15 millimetres long.
flow.context: In this step, you look at the sprouts and guess what will happen before you cut anything.

flow.do: Pick eight sprouts with straight roots. Label two plates A and B. Lay damp tissue on each. Put four sprouts on each plate, roots pointing the same way. Lay a thread along each root, then measure the thread. Write each length.
flow.say: Put four sprouts on plate A and four on plate B. Lay the thread along each root. Then measure the thread on the ruler. Write down every length.
flow.kid: Put four sprouts on each plate. Measure each root. Write it down.
flow.parent: Roots curve a little. A thread laid gently along the root and then measured on the ruler gives the real length. Do not pull the roots straight, because that can hurt them. Choose roots that are about the same length on both plates. Four roots per plate is few, and one root may stall, so use five per plate if you have them. With 2 to 4 children, each child sets up their own pair of plates (A and B) and measures their own roots, and at the end everyone adds their numbers together for a class average. With one child, the parent holds the thread and the child reads the ruler.

check.q: Why do we put sprouts from the same bunch on both plates?
options: So the only difference is the cut tip
Because we have no other seeds
So both plates look the same
check.why: Using the same seeds, tissue and place makes it a fair test. If the plates differ in only one way, the cut tip, then any difference in growth must come from that.

flow.context: In this step, you set up the two plates and measure every root before you cut.

flow.do: Wash your hands. A grown-up snips 3 millimetres off the tip of each root on plate B. On plate A, the grown-up only touches each tip with the closed scissors. Cover both plates with damp tissue and a lid. Put them side by side in a warm, dark place.
flow.say: A grown-up snips the very tip off the roots on plate B. On plate A, the scissors only touch. Why do we touch the roots on plate A?
flow.kid: A grown-up cuts the tips on plate B. On plate A, the scissors only touch.

ask.q: Why do we touch the roots on plate A with the scissors?
good: So both plates are handled the same way.
So the only difference is the missing tip.

flow.parent: 3 millimetres is about the width of a pencil's lead. Cut straight across. Both plates must stay together in the same place, so they have the same warmth and light. Check that the tissue stays damp.
flow.context: In this step, you cut the tips on one plate. You treat the other plate the same way, except for the cutting.

flow.do: After one day, take the lids off. Measure every root with the thread and the ruler. Write the numbers. Look closely at the cut roots. Drip a little water on the tissue and cover the plates again.
flow.say: It is one day later. Measure every root. Which plate has longer roots? What do you notice about the cut roots?
flow.kid: Measure every root. Write the lengths. Look at the cut roots closely.

ask.q: What do you notice about the cut roots on plate B?
good: A few have little bumps on the side.

flow.parent: Typical numbers, not promises: in warm weather uncut roots on plate A often grow about 10 to 25 millimetres in a day, and cut roots on plate B often grow only a few millimetres (about 0 to 8). The part just behind the cut can still stretch a little on the first day. If all roots on both plates grew the same, check that you cut the tip end of the root and not the end near the seed. In cool weather every root grows less, so compare plate with plate, not with these numbers. If you see white fuzz, rinse the tissue and use fresh tissue.

check.q: After one day, the roots on plate A grew a lot and the roots on plate B grew very little. What does this suggest?
options: The tip is where the root gets longer
Scissors make roots grow slower in the middle
check.why: Plate A and plate B were treated the same except for the tip. The root grew when its tip was there and hardly grew when the tip was cut. So the tip is where most of the lengthening happens. Plate B being colder would be a different explanation, which is why both plates stay side by side.

flow.context: In this step, you measure the roots after one day and write down how much each one grew.

flow.do: After two days, measure every root again. Work out how much each root grew. Add the growth of the four roots on each plate and divide by four. Draw one bar for each plate. Ask your child to say what they thought, what they saw and why.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What did you think would happen? What did you see? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Measure again. Find the average for each plate. Draw two bars. Say what you thought, what you saw and why.
flow.parent: A strong answer says that roots with the tip cut off grew much less, that the tip is where new cells are made by dividing, that just behind the tip those cells stretch and make the root longer, and that further back the root has finished growing. Do not give this answer first. Let your child say what they saw, then add the words cell division. If your results are not clear, write them as they are, and try again with a new bunch.
flow.think: A farmer's goat nibbles the very tips of a row of young roots. What would you expect to happen to the roots?
flow.context: In this step, you measure for the last time, find the average growth for each plate, and explain what it shows.

experiments.title: Dots on a Root: how far does the growing zone reach?
experiments.question: If you mark dots along a growing root, which gaps between the dots grow wider after a day?
experiments.predict: Before you mark the roots, guess. Will all the gaps grow wider, or only some? Which ones? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Each root gets the same row of dots, 2 millimetres apart, starting at the tip. All roots stay on the same plate in the same place. The gaps along one root are compared with each other, so the root is its own control. You also leave one root without dots, to check that the dots do not stop it growing.
results_table: Where it is on the root

materials.item: 4 sprouted moong seeds with straight roots at least 20 millimetres long (from the Cut the Tip test, or a new batch)
a fine-tip waterproof marker, or a toothpick dipped in kajal or ink
a toothpick and a little kajal or ink, as a backup if the marker will not mark a damp root
a ruler marked in millimetres
a plate, kitchen tissue and a lid
a magnifying glass, if you have one
a card or paper with a ruler line drawn on it, marked at 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 and 11 millimetres

schedule.what: Guess, mark the dots on the roots and lay the roots on damp tissue.
Measure the gaps between the dots and find where the growing happened.

experiments.safety: Use a fine pen with waterproof ink, and keep it away from your mouth. Wash hands after handling the sprouts. Do not eat sprouts that have been marked.
experiments.record: Write the length of each gap at the start and after one day. Work out the change. Draw a bar for each gap, from the tip backward.
experiments.context: This is a follow-up to Cut the Tip. In Cut the Tip, you found that a root hardly grows without its tip. Here you find how far back from the tip the growing reaches.

setup.art: A moong sprout lying on a ruler card with small tick marks, its pale tip at the zero end.
setup.caption: 1. Lay a root on the marked card with its tip at the zero line.

setup.art: A hand touching a fine pen to the root at the first tick mark, with six small dots in a row along the root.
setup.caption: 2. Make six small dots at 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 and 11 millimetres from the tip.

setup.art: The marked sprouts lying on damp tissue on a plate under a lid.
setup.caption: 3. Lay the sprouts on damp tissue. Cover them and wait one day.

setup.art: A magnifying glass held over the root, with the gaps between dots now different widths and the first gaps wider.
setup.caption: 4. After a day, measure the gaps between the dots again.

flow.do: Look at a root with your child. Ask for a guess and a reason, and write both down.
flow.say: We will put six dots along a root, two millimetres apart. Tomorrow the root will be longer. Will all the gaps grow wider? Or only some? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: We will put six dots on a root. Will all the gaps grow wider? Why?

ask.q: Which gap do you think will grow the most?

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. If your child did Cut the Tip, they may guess that the gap nearest the tip grows most. Ask why they think so. With 2 to 4 children, each child marks one root and measures it, and the group compares roots. With one child, the parent dries the roots and the child makes the dots.
flow.context: This is the first step of Dots on a Root. You guess before you mark anything.

flow.do: Dry one root gently with tissue. Lay it next to the marked card with the tip at zero. Touch a fine pen to the root at 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 and 11 millimetres. Make small dots. Do the same for two more roots. Leave the fourth root without dots, to check that the dots do not stop the growing.
flow.say: Dry the root with tissue first. Lay the tip at zero on the card. Touch the pen very lightly at each mark. Make small dots, not lines.
flow.kid: Dry the root. Lay it on the card. Make six small dots with the pen.
flow.parent: This is the fussy step. A wet root does not hold ink. Dab dry, mark in a second, then put it straight back on damp tissue. If the dots smear or fade, use a toothpick dipped in kajal and touch it to the root. If a root breaks, set it aside and use another.
flow.context: In this step, you mark the dots along the root. They are the marks you will measure from.

flow.do: Lay the roots on damp tissue on a plate. Cover with a lid. Keep the plate in a warm, dark place for one day.
flow.say: Lay the roots back on damp tissue. Cover them. Leave them for one day.
flow.kid: Lay the roots on damp tissue. Cover them. Wait one day.
flow.wait: Leave the plate for one day.
flow.context: In this step, you leave the marked roots to grow for one day.

flow.do: After one day, measure each gap between the dots. Start at the tip and go backward. Write the gaps in the table. Work out how much each gap changed. Draw a bar for each gap. Ask your child to say what they thought, what they saw and why.
flow.say: Measure each gap, starting at the tip. Which gaps grew? Which stayed the same? Why do you think the growing happened where it did?
flow.kid: Measure each gap from the tip back. Which gaps grew? Which stayed the same?
flow.parent: Typical results, not promises: the first one or two gaps next to the tip grow the most. The next gaps grow a little. Gaps more than about 1 centimetre from the tip hardly change. Dots are tiny, so use a magnifier, or measure how far each dot is from the tip and subtract one number from the next. Dots may fade, so measure the same day. Compare the total growth of the unmarked root with a marked one: they should be about the same. If the dots washed off or the roots dried out, say so, and try again with kajal and a fresh root. A fuzzy result is still a result.

check.q: The gaps nearest the tip grew wider, and the gaps far from the tip stayed the same. What does this show?
options: Only a short zone near the tip lengthens
The seed pushes the root out
check.why: If the whole root stretched evenly, every gap would grow by the same share. Only the gaps close to the tip grew, so growing is limited to a short zone near the end. A seed pushing the root would move all the dots the same way, without changing the gaps.

flow.context: In this step, you measure the gaps and find where the growing happened.

activities.title: Fold and Count: how fast does doubling grow?

materials.item: 2 large sheets of newspaper or one sheet of A4 paper for each fold test
a pencil and a marker
a calculator or a pencil and paper for the sums

activities.safety: Handle paper carefully. Fold slowly so that you do not get paper cuts.
activities.record: Write the number of boxes after each fold. Then write the table for 10, 20, 30 and 45 doublings. Draw a line to show how it climbs.
activities.context: In this activity, you fold paper in half again and again, as a cell divides into two. You count the boxes and then work out how many doublings it takes to make a body.

setup.art: A big sheet of newspaper lying flat, with a marker writing the number 1 in the middle.
setup.caption: 1. One sheet is one cell. Write 1.

setup.art: The sheet folded in half, then opened, showing two boxes, and then folded again showing four boxes.
setup.caption: 2. Fold in half. Open it. Count the boxes. Fold again.

setup.art: A table with the number of folds on the left and the number of boxes on the right, doubling each time.
setup.caption: 3. Write the number of boxes after each fold in a table.

flow.do: Lay the sheet flat. Draw one dot in the middle. Say that this sheet is one cell. Ask for a guess about how many boxes there will be after 5 folds.
flow.say: This sheet is one cell. When a cell divides, she becomes two. I fold the paper in half. How many boxes will there be after five folds?
flow.kid: This sheet is one cell. Fold it in half. How many boxes after five folds?
flow.parent: Most children guess 5 or 10. The real answer is 32, so the guess teaches a lot.
flow.context: This is the first step of Fold and Count. You guess how fast the number grows.

flow.do: Fold the paper in half. Open it and count the boxes. Write the number in a table. Fold again in the same direction, open, count and write. Do this up to six folds.
flow.say: Fold in half. Open it. Count the boxes. Write the number. Fold again and count again.
flow.kid: Fold. Open. Count the boxes. Write the number. Do it up to six folds.

ask.q: What pattern do you see in the numbers?
good: Each number is double the one before.

flow.parent: After 6 folds there are 64 boxes. A seventh fold is nearly impossible by hand. That is a good moment to say that a real cell does not have to fold anything, so nothing like the thickness of paper limits her. She can divide again and again. With 2 to 4 children, each child folds a sheet and a different child writes down the table. Then compare: does everyone get the same numbers?
flow.context: In this step, you fold six times and write down how many boxes there are each time.

flow.do: Use the pattern to fill in a second table. 10 doublings give 1,024. 20 doublings give 1,048,576. 30 doublings give about 1,073 million. 45 doublings give about 35 trillion. Say that a body has about 30 to 40 trillion cells. Ask for a reason that the number grows so fast.
flow.say: Ten doublings give 1,024. Twenty give about one million. Thirty give about one billion. Forty-five give about thirty-five trillion. That is close to the number of cells in a body.
flow.kid: Ten doublings make 1,024. Forty-five doublings make about 35 trillion. That is a whole body!
flow.parent: Compare with real cells. A bacterium that divided every 20 minutes without stopping would have about a billion descendants after 10 hours (30 doublings). In real life food and space run out long before that.
flow.think: A body takes at least 45 doublings from one cell. Why do you think it takes many more divisions in real life?

check.q: About how many doublings of one cell would it take to reach 35 trillion cells?
check.why: Each doubling multiplies the number by 2. After 10 doublings you have about a thousand. After 20 about a million, and after 30 about a billion. After 45 you reach about 35 trillion. It does not take anywhere near 350 doublings.

flow.context: In this step, you extend the pattern to see how many doublings it takes to make a body.

activities.title: Copy Machine: can you copy a long code without a mistake?

materials.item: 2 sheets of paper, a pencil and an eraser
a clock or a timer on a phone
a parent or a friend to check

activities.record: Write the number of mistakes in your first copy and in your checked copy. Draw the matching strand for your code.
activities.context: In this activity, you copy a long code of four letters by hand, the way a cell copies DNA. You count your mistakes, and then you find out how a cell checks her copy.

setup.art: A strip of paper with a 40-letter code made of A, T, C and G in four colours.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up writes a 40-letter code using A, T, C and G.

setup.art: A child copying the code onto a second line with a timer showing 2 minutes.
setup.caption: 2. Copy the code in 2 minutes. Work carefully.

setup.art: A parent checking two lines with a finger, circling two letters that do not match.
setup.caption: 3. The checker compares the lines and circles mistakes.

setup.art: Under each letter of the code a matching partner letter is written, A under T, and C under G.
setup.caption: 4. Write the partner letter under each letter: A with T, and C with G.

flow.do: Write this code on a strip of paper for your child: ATTCGGATCCAGTTAGCTAGGCTAATCGGATCATGCTAAG. Explain the four letters. Ask for a guess about how many mistakes a copy will have.
flow.say: A cell's instructions are written in four letters, A, T, C and G. Here is a short piece. Copy it exactly. How many mistakes do you think you will make?
flow.kid: Here is a code of four letters. Copy it exactly. How many mistakes will you make?
flow.parent: This code is 40 letters long. You can make your own, as long as it uses only A, T, C and G.
flow.context: This is the first step of Copy Machine. You get the code to copy and make a guess.

flow.do: Start the timer for 2 minutes. Your child copies the code onto a new line. Stop when the time is up. Compare the two lines letter by letter and circle the mistakes. Count them.
flow.say: Copy the code. You have two minutes. Now I will check every letter. Let us count the mistakes.
flow.kid: Copy the code in two minutes. Your helper checks it. Count the mistakes.

ask.q: Were the mistakes near the start, middle or end?
good: Near the end, when I got tired.

flow.parent: Some children make no mistake in 40 letters. If so, make a longer code of 120 letters and try again. Repeated letters like GG and TT are where mistakes happen most. With 2 to 4 children, everyone copies the same code at the same time, then swap papers and check each other's copy. Compare who made the fewest mistakes and where.
flow.context: In this step, you copy once and count your mistakes.

flow.do: Your child now copies the code again, in a new line, and reads each letter aloud while checking against the original. Compare again and count mistakes.
flow.say: Now copy again. This time check each letter with the original before you write the next. How many mistakes now?
flow.kid: Copy again. Check each letter as you go. Count the mistakes.
flow.parent: Cells have proofreading machines. They check each new letter as it is added, and they repair most mistakes. Mistakes that get past are rare but they are the source of small differences between cells.
flow.context: In this step, you copy again with a proofreading check, as cells do.

flow.do: Write the partner letter under each letter of the code: A with T, and C with G. Then cover the top line and copy the code using only the partner line. Compare it with the original.
flow.say: A cell has a matching partner for each letter. A goes with T. C goes with G. Write the partners. Now cover the top line. Can you rebuild it from the partners?
flow.kid: A goes with T. C goes with G. Write the partners. Cover the top. Rebuild it.
flow.parent: The idea that each side of DNA can rebuild the other was suggested by Watson and Crick in 1953. They used the X-ray pictures taken by Rosalind Franklin and her student Raymond Gosling, and some of Franklin's data was shown to Watson without her knowing. A cell copies about 6 billion letters each time she divides, and makes only a handful of mistakes.
flow.think: DNA is like a ladder, and each side of the ladder can rebuild the other. Why does the cell unzip the ladder before copying?
flow.context: In this step, you write the partner strand and use it to rebuild the code, which is how DNA is copied.

activities.title: Skin Flakes: catch some of your own cells

materials.item: clear sticky tape, 3 centimetres long, 6 pieces (3 places, and a second piece for each place)
a sheet of black paper or dark cloth
a magnifying glass, if you have one
a mirror or window light, and a pencil for notes

activities.safety: Use clean, unbroken skin only. Do not tape over sore, red, rashy or cut skin, or over thick hair. Peel the tape off slowly. Stop if the skin hurts.
activities.record: Draw what you see under the tape. Write which place on your body gave the most flakes.
activities.context: In this activity, you lift a layer of dry skin with sticky tape, and look at it on dark paper. You see some of the cells that your body has already finished with.

setup.art: A strip of clear tape being pressed on the back of a child's forearm.
setup.caption: 1. Press a strip of tape on dry skin. Rub it lightly.

setup.art: The tape being peeled off slowly and then stuck onto black paper.
setup.caption: 2. Peel off the tape slowly. Stick it on black paper.

setup.art: A hand holding a magnifying glass over the tape, showing a cloudy patch with tiny flakes.
setup.caption: 3. Look closely. Use a magnifier if you have one.

flow.do: Choose three places, such as the back of the hand, the forearm and the heel. Ask your child to guess which one will give the most skin flakes. Plan to score each strip from 0 (clear) to 3 (very cloudy).
flow.say: We will lift some skin from three places. Which place do you think will give the most? Why?
flow.kid: Pick three places on your skin. Which will give the most flakes? Why?
flow.parent: The heel and elbow often give the most because they are thick and dry. Do not use any place with a rash or sore.
flow.context: This is the first step of Skin Flakes. You choose places and guess.

flow.do: For each place, press a strip of tape on the skin and rub it lightly for 5 seconds. Peel it off slowly. Stick it on black paper. Write the place under each strip. Then press a second, fresh strip on the exact same spot and do the same. Score every strip from 0 to 3 for cloudiness, with a magnifier if you have one.
flow.say: Press the tape on your skin. Rub it. Peel it off slowly. Stick it on black paper. What do you see on the tape?
flow.kid: Press tape on your skin. Peel it off slowly. Stick it on black paper.

ask.q: What do you think those flakes are?
good: Pieces of the top of my skin.

ask.q: Do you think those cells were alive?
good: The top layer is dead cells.

flow.parent: You will not see single cells. You will see a cloudy or whitish patch and small flakes, mixed with a few hairs and specks of dust. Each flake is a sheet of many flat cells, so a pinhead of skin holds thousands. Dry places such as the heel, elbow or shin show the most. If you see almost nothing on soft or oily skin, that is normal: try a drier place and rub for 10 seconds. The second strip on the same spot usually shows less, because the first strip already took the loosest flakes. The top layer of skin is made of dead cells, and new cells keep pushing up from below. Scientists estimate that a person loses roughly 30,000 to 40,000 dead skin cells every minute. With 2 to 4 children, each child tapes their own arm and compares scores.
flow.think: If your top skin is replaced about every month, where do the new cells come from?

check.q: The flakes on the tape are mostly...
options: Dead cells from the top of the skin
check.why: The top layer of skin is made of cells that have finished their work and died. They are tough and flat, and they rub off all the time. New cells push up from below to take their place. Living cells deep inside are not on the surface.

flow.context: In this step, you lift flakes of skin with tape and look at them.

activities.title: Paper Chromosomes: act out how one cell becomes two

materials.item: 12 strips of coloured paper or card, 3 colours with 4 strips of each
tape or rubber bands
2 plates or bowls
a long piece of string
a pen
a pair of scissors for cutting the strips

activities.record: Draw the four steps of mitosis in order. Write a sentence under each one.
activities.context: In this activity, you use paper strips for chromosomes. You copy them, line them up, pull them apart and share them between two bowls, as a dividing cell does.

setup.art: Six paper strips in three colours, two of each colour, lying inside a large circle drawn on paper.
setup.caption: 1. Six strips are the chromosomes in one cell. Lay them in a circle.

setup.art: Each strip now paired with an identical copy, taped in the middle to form an X shape.
setup.caption: 2. Make a copy of each strip. Tape each pair in the middle.

setup.art: The six X shapes in a straight line along a string across the middle of the paper.
setup.caption: 3. Line the X shapes up along the string.

setup.art: Two hands pulling the halves of each X apart to opposite ends, into two bowls.
setup.caption: 4. Pull each X apart. Put one half in each bowl.

flow.do: Cut six strips: two red, two blue and two green. Lay them in a large circle drawn on paper. Say that the strips are chromosomes, and that this is one cell. Each colour is a pair.
flow.say: These strips are chromosomes. This circle is a cell. There are three pairs, one red pair, one blue pair and one green pair. This cell will divide.
flow.kid: The strips are chromosomes. The circle is a cell. This cell will divide.
flow.parent: A real human cell has 46 chromosomes, which is 23 pairs. Six is just enough to show the idea.
flow.context: This is the first step of Paper Chromosomes. You set up the cell.

flow.do: Cut a matching copy of each strip, in the same colour. Tape each strip to its copy in the middle, so it looks like an X. You now have six X shapes.
flow.say: Before a cell divides, she copies every chromosome. Tape each strip to its copy in the middle. Now there are six X shapes.
flow.kid: Copy every strip. Tape each pair in the middle to make an X.

check.q: Why does the cell copy her chromosomes before she splits?
options: So each daughter cell can get a full set
Because copying is faster than splitting
check.why: If the cell split without copying, each daughter would get only half of the instructions. Copying first means there is a full set to give to each daughter.

flow.context: In this step, you copy the chromosomes first, as the cell does before dividing.

flow.do: Lay the string across the middle of the circle. Line up all six X shapes along the string. Say that this is the line-up step.
flow.say: Line the X shapes up along the string, in the middle of the cell. This is the line-up step.
flow.kid: Line the six X shapes up along the string.
flow.context: In this step, you line the copied chromosomes up across the middle of the cell.

flow.do: Pull each X apart at the tape. Put one half of each X in one bowl and the other half in the other bowl. Count the strips in each bowl. Then play it again, but this time drop both halves of one green X in the same bowl. Count again.
flow.say: Now pull each X apart. One half goes in each bowl. Count the strips. Then try a mistake. Put both halves of one green X in the same bowl. What goes wrong?
flow.kid: Pull each X apart. One half goes to each bowl. Count the strips in each bowl.

ask.q: What goes wrong if both halves of one green X go into the same bowl?
good: One cell has too many, and one has none.
One cell is missing a green chromosome.
The cells would not be the same.

flow.parent: A correct split puts 6 strips in each bowl, two of each colour. The mistake gives 7 in one and 5 in the other. Real mistakes like this cause some illnesses that people are born with. A cell's spindle threads pull each chromosome pair very carefully so that mistakes are rare. With 2 to 4 children, give each child one colour pair to pull apart, and let one child hold each bowl.
flow.think: Which would be worse for a cell: one chromosome too many, or one chromosome too few?
flow.context: In this step, you pull the copies apart into two bowls, and see what happens if the sharing goes wrong.

activities.safety: Use blunt child scissors, or let a grown-up cut the strips. Keep tape and rubber bands away from the mouth.

projects.title: Pinch the Tulsi: what happens when you pinch a growing tip?

materials.item: a tulsi (holy basil) plant in a pot with two or more stems of about the same height (mint, basil or chilli also work)
2 pieces of coloured thread to label stems
a ruler marked in centimetres
a notebook and a pencil

projects.safety: Wash hands after handling the plant. Do not eat leaves from a plant that has been sprayed with anything. Tulsi is sacred in many homes, so ask the elders before you pinch it, or use mint or basil instead.

schedule.what: Choose two similar stems. Tie a red thread on stem A and a blue thread on stem B. Measure and draw both. Pinch off the top two leaves of stem A. Leave stem B alone.
Measure both stems. Look at the places where leaves join the stem. Draw what you see.
Measure both stems. Count the small side shoots on each. Draw both stems.
Measure both stems. Count the side shoots on each. Draw both stems. Say what happened and why.

projects.record: Write the height of each stem and the number of side shoots on days 1, 4, 7 and 14. Draw the two stems side by side on each day.
projects.context: In this project, you pinch the tip off one stem of a tulsi plant and leave another stem alone. You find out what happens when the growing tip is removed.

setup.art: Two stems of a tulsi plant, one tied with a red thread and one with a blue thread, with a ruler beside the pot.
setup.caption: 1. Tie a thread on two similar stems. Measure both.

setup.art: Fingers pinching off the two top leaves of the red-thread stem, while the blue-thread stem is left whole.
setup.caption: 2. Pinch off the top two leaves of the red stem only.

setup.art: A week later: the pinched stem has two small side shoots, and the unpinched stem is taller with none.
setup.caption: 3. After a week, look at both stems and count the side shoots.

flow.do: Choose two similar stems. Tie a red thread on one and a blue thread on the other. Measure and draw both. Ask for a guess and a reason about what will happen when you pinch the red stem's tip.
flow.say: We will pinch the top two leaves of the red stem and leave the blue one alone. What do you think will happen? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Pinch the top of the red stem. Leave the blue stem. What will happen? Why?

ask.q: What do you think will happen to the red stem?

flow.parent: Pinch off the top bud and the two small leaves under it, using your fingertips. Pinch cleanly. Choose stems without flowers. Many families pinch tulsi to keep it bushy, so it is safe for the plant. Growth is slow below about 15 degrees C, so in a cold winter wait for warmer weather or use a plant kept indoors in good light. With 2 to 4 children, give each child their own pair of stems (or their own cheap pot of mint) and compare the results on day 14.
flow.context: This is the first step of Pinch the Tulsi. You set up two stems and guess what will happen.

flow.do: Day 4. Measure both stems. Look at the places where the leaves join the stem. Draw what you see.
flow.say: Measure both stems. Look where each leaf joins the stem. Do you see anything new?
flow.kid: Measure both stems. Look where leaves join the stem.
flow.context: In this step, you check the two stems after three days.

flow.do: Day 7. Measure both stems. Count the small side shoots on each. Draw both stems.
flow.say: Count the new side shoots on each stem. Which has more? What do you think made the difference?
flow.kid: Count the side shoots on each stem. Which has more?
flow.context: In this step, you check the stems after a week and count the side shoots.

flow.do: Day 14. Measure both stems and count the side shoots again. Ask your child to say what they thought, what they saw and why.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What did you think would happen? What did you see? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Measure and count again. Say what you thought, what you saw and why.
flow.parent: Typical result: the pinched stem grows side shoots at the leaf joints within a week, and ends up bushier but not taller. The unpinched stem grows taller with few side shoots. The tip makes a chemical signal, called auxin, that holds back the side buds. Remove the tip and the signal stops, so the side buds wake up. This was studied by Kenneth Thimann and Folke Skoog in 1933. If nothing happens, wait a few more days, because slow plants take longer, and check that you pinched the very tip and gave the plant light and water.
flow.think: A gardener pinches a tulsi plant every week. What shape will the plant grow into?
flow.context: In this step, you finish the project and explain what pinching did.

challenges.title: The Longest Root: design the best home for a growing root
challenges.problem: You want a moong root to grow as long as possible in two days. Design a home for the sprouts using only things in your kitchen, and test it against a plain plate.
constraints: Use only things you have at home.
Use the same number of seeds and the same seed type in each home.
Measure the longest root in each home after two days.
materials: plates, katoris, a glass jar or a tumbler
kitchen tissue, a cotton cloth or a sponge
a steel lunch box or a cardboard box
a spray bottle or a spoon for water
general: Lay the sprouts on damp tissue on a plate. Cover with a lid. Keep in a warm, dark cupboard.
Roll the sprouts in a damp cloth and put the roll in a bowl. Sprinkle water twice a day.
Put the sprouts in a steel lunch box with damp tissue at the bottom, with the lid slightly open.
creative: Stand a strip of tissue in a tumbler with a little water at the bottom. Lay the seeds on the tissue so that the roots can grow downward along it.
Place the sprouts on a sponge in a tray with a little water, so the sponge keeps the roots damp but not drowned.
Tilt a plate on a book so extra water drains away. Roots need air as well as water.

setup.art: A plain plate with four sprouts on damp tissue, beside a second home made from a rolled damp cloth in a bowl.
setup.caption: 1. Make two different homes. Put four sprouts in each.

setup.art: Both homes side by side in a warm, dark cupboard, with labels A and B.
setup.caption: 2. Keep both homes together in the same warm, dark place.

setup.art: A child measuring the longest root in each home with a thread and a ruler.
setup.caption: 3. After two days, measure the longest root in each home.

challenges.your_turn: Make two different homes with four seeds in each. Keep both in the same warm place. After two days, measure the longest root in each. Which home won? Why do you think it did?
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. You use what you learned about roots to make the best home for a growing root, and you test your design against a plain plate.

flow.do: Look at the materials. Ask your child to say what a root needs to grow. Write the list.
flow.say: What does a growing root need? Think of water, warmth, air and darkness. We will design two homes and test them.
flow.kid: What does a root need? Water, warmth, air. Make a list.

ask.q: What does a root need in order to grow?

flow.parent: A root drowned in water gets too little air and grows poorly. A root dried out stops growing. The best home is damp, not wet.
flow.context: This is the first step of The Longest Root. You think about what a root needs.

flow.do: Make two different homes. Put four seeds with tiny roots in each. Label them. Measure the longest root in each home and write it.
flow.say: Make two homes that are different from each other. Put four seeds in each. Label them. Measure the longest root in each.
flow.kid: Make two homes. Put four seeds in each. Label them. Measure the roots.
flow.context: In this step, you build the two homes and measure the roots at the start.

flow.do: After two days, measure the longest root in each home. Write the numbers. Decide which home won. Ask your child to say why.
flow.say: Measure the longest root in each home. Which home won? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Measure the longest root in each home. Which won? Why?
flow.parent: A good answer talks about the roots being damp but not drowned, warm and in the dark. A fair test means the number of seeds, the place and the time are the same.
flow.think: What would you change in your design if you made it again?
flow.context: In this step, you measure again and explain which home was best.

items.p: How does a cell make a new cell?
opts: By copying her instructions and splitting into two
By growing out of non-living material
By taking pieces from other cells and joining them
items.why: Every cell comes from a cell that divided. She copies her instructions, shares the copies, and splits into two daughter cells. No one has ever seen a cell form from non-living material.

items.p: When a cell divides, the old cell is left behind as a dead body.
items.why: False. The cell does not die. She becomes the two daughter cells, and nothing is left behind.

items.p: Put the steps of cell division in the right order.
a: The cell copies all her chromosomes
The copies line up across the middle of the cell
Threads pull the copies apart to the two ends
The cell pinches in two, or builds a wall across the middle
items.why: Copying must come first, so each daughter can get a full set. The pulling comes before the split. Splitting comes last.

items.p: Before a cell divides, she must make a copy of her ____.
items.why: If a cell split before copying, each daughter would get only half of the instructions.

items.p: Why do the copied chromosomes line up in the middle of the cell before they are pulled apart?
opts: So that one copy of each can be pulled to each end
So that the cell can store them
So that the cell can become bigger
items.why: Lining up puts each pair where threads can pull one copy each way. Then each daughter gets exactly one full set.

items.p: A root with its tip cut off hardly grows longer, but a root left alone does. What does this suggest?
opts: Cells dividing at the tip make most of the new length
The tip is the only part that drinks water
Cutting makes roots weaker for ever
items.why: The two roots differed only in the tip. So the tip is where most of the lengthening comes from. Cells divide there and then stretch a little.

items.p: A root grows longer evenly along its whole length, like a rubber band stretching.
items.why: False. Dots marked along a growing root show that only the part within a few millimetres of the tip lengthens. The rest stays the same length.

items.p: Match each kind of cell to how she finishes dividing.
pairs: grows a bud that breaks off
builds a new wall across the middle
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: All these cells copy their instructions and split, but they finish in different ways. A plant cell has a stiff wall, so she builds a new wall. An animal cell has no wall, so she pinches.

items.p: What is a fertilised egg?
opts: The first cell of a new animal, which divides to make the whole body
A cell that cannot divide
The last cell to form in a body
items.why: A fertilised egg is made when a sperm cell joins an egg cell. She divides again and again, and her daughters take on different jobs.

items.p: Sort each item: is it the same in a muscle cell and a skin cell, or different?
items: Which pages of the instruction book are used
The letters of DNA in the nucleus
items.a: as given
items.why: Both cells came from one fertilised egg, so they hold the same instructions. They look different and work differently because they use different pages of the same book.

items.p: Which of these is replaced fastest in a grown person?
opts: The lining of the gut
Cells in the middle of the eye lens
Nerve cells in the thinking part of the brain
items.why: The gut lining is replaced about every 3 to 5 days. The eye lens centre and the nerve cells in the cortex last for a whole life.

items.p: Cells that meet the outside world, such as skin and the gut lining, are often replaced ____ than cells deep inside.
items.why: The outside world scrapes and wears these cells, and so they are replaced fast. Cells deep inside are better protected and can last for years.

items.p: A bacterium divides into two every 30 minutes. Start with 1 bacterium. How many are there after 2 hours?
items.why: 2 hours is four periods of 30 minutes. 1 doubles four times: 2, 4, 8, 16. So there are 16 bacteria.

items.p: Explain in your own words why a root gets longer only at its tip.
items.a: At the tip, cells divide again and again and the new cells stretch a little. Behind the tip the cells have finished. They do not divide, so that part stays the same length.
items.why: A strong answer says that cells divide at the tip, that the new cells make the new length, and that the older part behind the tip does not lengthen.

items.p: Draw four small pictures to show a cell dividing in order. Write one word under each picture.
items.a: A round cell with threads in a nucleus, then a cell with X-shaped chromosomes lined up in the middle, then the chromosomes pulled to the two ends, then two separate cells. Words such as copy, line up, pull, split.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the chromosomes copied first, lined up, pulled apart to opposite ends, and then two cells.

items.p: Your skin is replaced about every month, yet it never wears thin. Why?
items.a: New cells are made under the top layer all the time, as fast as old cells flake off. The top layer is made of finished cells, and new ones keep pushing up from below.
items.why: A strong answer says that cells divide in the lower layer and rise up, so the number of cells stays about the same.

items.p: What is the job of the spindle threads in a dividing cell?
opts: To pull the copied chromosomes apart to the two ends
To copy the DNA
To make a new cell wall
items.why: The spindle threads attach to each chromosome and pull the two copies in opposite directions. This is how each daughter cell gets one full set.

items.p: A human cell has 46 chromosomes. How many does each daughter cell get after normal mitosis?
items.why: The cell copies her chromosomes to 92 and then shares them equally. Each daughter gets 46, the same as the cell she came from.

items.p: A grown-up red blood cell can divide, because she holds the full set of instructions.
items.why: False. A red blood cell loses her nucleus when she is made, so she cannot divide. New red blood cells are made by stem cells in the marrow.

items.p: The caps at the ends of chromosomes, which get shorter each time a cell divides, are called ____.
items.why: Telomeres protect the ends of chromosomes. When they get very short, a normal cell stops dividing.

items.p: Match each part of the body to how quickly its cells are replaced.
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Cells that are scraped and worn by the outside world are replaced fastest. Protected cells last much longer. The cells in the middle of the lens were made before you were born.

items.p: A cell divides once a day. Each daughter also divides once a day. Start with 1 cell. How many cells are there after 8 days?
items.why: The number doubles every day: 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256. So there are 256 cells after 8 days.

items.p: The lining of the gut is replaced about every 4 days. About how many times is it replaced in one year of 365 days?
items.a: About 90 times
items.why: 365 divided by 4 is about 91. So the gut lining is renewed about 90 times a year. This is a rough answer, because the time varies.

items.p: Sort each kind of cell: does she keep dividing in a grown person, or almost never?
items: Stem cells in the gut lining
Nerve cells in the thinking part of the brain
Cells in the middle of the eye lens
items.a: as given
items.why: Stem cells in the marrow, gut and skin keep making new cells all your life. Nerve cells in the cortex, lens cells and heart muscle cells divide very rarely or not at all.

items.p: Put these in order, from fewest cells to most cells.
items.why: A fertilised egg is 1 cell. After three rounds of division there are 8. A few days later the group is a hollow ball of many more cells. A newborn baby has trillions.

items.p: Which one is the odd one out, and why? Mitosis, binary fission, budding, photosynthesis.
items.a: Photosynthesis, because it is how plants make food from light. The other three are ways that cells divide.
items.why: Mitosis, binary fission and budding are all ways one cell becomes two. Photosynthesis is a different process, which makes sugar using sunlight.

items.p: You put dots 2 millimetres apart along a growing root. After a day, only the gaps near the tip are wider. Which statement fits?
opts: Lengthening happens in a short zone near the tip
The whole root stretched evenly
The dots near the tip fell off
items.why: If the whole root stretched evenly, every gap would be wider. Only the gaps near the tip grew, so the growing zone is short and close to the end.

items.p: John Gurdon put the nucleus of a frog's gut cell into an egg and got a tadpole. What does this tell us about the gut cell?
items.a: The gut cell still held the whole set of instructions for the entire frog. She used only the gut pages, but the other pages were still in her nucleus.
items.why: A strong answer says that a specialised cell keeps all the instructions, even though she uses only some.

items.p: A friend says: 'All the cells in my body are replaced every seven years, so I'm a completely new person.' What would you say, and why?
items.a: Different cells last different times. Gut cells last days, but many nerve cells and lens cells last a whole life. So there is no one number, and some of you is as old as you are.
items.why: A strong answer says that cell lifetimes vary a lot, that some cells are never replaced, and that the seven-year rule is a myth.

items.p: Draw a plant cell and an animal cell, each at the end of division. Show how they finish differently.
items.a: An animal cell pinched into two with a narrowing waist, and a plant cell with a new wall across the middle.
items.why: A strong drawing shows an animal cell pinching and a plant cell building a wall.

items.p: Skin cells are all replaced about every month. Is it still your own skin?

views.says: A hedge that is trimmed and regrows is still the same hedge. It keeps its place and its shape, so your skin does too.
If every plank of a ship is replaced, we keep the name but we may not have the same ship. Maybe your skin is a new skin each month.
Not all of you is replaced at once. Some cells stay for life, and your instructions are copied again and again. The pattern continues, even though the pieces change.

items.ask: Which view makes most sense to you? What would make you change your mind?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer picks a view, gives a reason, and says what would change the child's mind, such as learning how much stays and how much changes.
items.why: This question has no single right answer. Each view picks out something real: the shape that continues, the pieces that change, or the instructions that are copied.

items.p: Identical twins can form when the early group of cells splits in two and each group grows into a baby.
items.why: True. Early cells in the embryo can separate into two groups. Each group can develop into a whole body with the same instructions.

items.p: Explain how one fertilised egg can become a body with skin, muscle and nerve cells, if every cell began with the same instructions.
items.a: The egg divides many times, and her daughters get the same full set of instructions. Signals from the cells around each daughter decide which pages she uses. Skin cells use skin pages, and muscle cells use muscle pages. So the cells look and work differently although they hold the same book.
items.why: A strong answer says that cells copy the full set of instructions and use different parts of them, depending on signals from the cells around them.

items.p: A cell divides once a day, and each daughter divides once a day too. Start with 1 cell. How many cells are there after 10 days?
items.why: The number doubles every day. 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256, 512, and then 1,024 on day 10. So there are 1,024 cells.

items.p: Your marrow makes about 2 million red blood cells every second. About how many is that in one minute?
items.a: 120 million
items.why: There are 60 seconds in a minute. 2 million times 60 is 120 million. So marrow makes about 120 million red blood cells every minute.

items.p: After the bomb tests of the 1950s and 1960s, the air carried extra carbon-14. Scientists use the carbon-14 in a cell's DNA to tell how old she is. Why does this work?
opts: Her DNA was built in the year she was made, from carbon with that year's level of carbon-14
Carbon-14 is made by the cell herself
Carbon-14 makes cells divide
items.why: The carbon in food comes from plants, which take it from the air. A cell's DNA is built when she is made, so it holds the carbon-14 level of that year. Older and younger cells carry different levels.

items.p: A cell that ends up with an extra copy of a chromosome after dividing always works better.
items.why: False. A cell needs exactly one full set. An extra chromosome or a missing one upsets the balance of her instructions, and may cause illness.

items.p: Which is the odd one out, and why? Gut lining, skin, red blood cells, cells in the middle of the eye lens.
items.a: The cells in the middle of the eye lens, because they are not replaced in a lifetime. The other three are replaced in days to months.
items.why: Gut lining, skin and red blood cells are replaced regularly. The cells in the middle of the lens are made before birth and stay for life.

items.p: John Gurdon grew a tadpole from the nucleus of a frog's gut cell. This showed that a specialised cell, such as a gut cell, still holds a full ____ of instructions.
items.why: The tadpole grew because the gut cell's nucleus held every instruction needed for a whole frog.

items.p: Match each finding to what it suggests.
pairs: Roots with the tip cut off stop lengthening
Cells at the tip make the new length
Flakes lifted from skin by tape
The top layer is made of finished cells
Muscle and skin share the same DNA
Cells use different pages of one book
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each finding points to an idea. Cutting a tip shows where lengthening starts. Skin flakes show cells wearing off. Sharing DNA shows that cells choose pages. Ignored stop signals show that division is normally controlled.

items.p: In a Cut the Tip test, the roots with cut tips were kept in the fridge and the roots with their tips on were kept on a shelf. The cut roots grew less. Why does this not show that the tip matters?
opts: Cold could have slowed the cut roots, so two things were different at once
Scissors are not allowed in tests
Roots should never be cut
items.why: A fair test changes only one thing. Here the tip and the temperature were both different. So you cannot tell which one caused the slower growth.

items.p: Put these steps of a new person's beginning in order, earliest first.
a: A sperm cell joins an egg cell
The fertilised egg divides into 2, 4, 8 cells
The cells take on different jobs
items.why: The egg must be fertilised before she divides. Division comes before the cells take on different jobs. The baby is born many weeks later.

items.p: Cancer begins when a cell ignores the stop signals. Explain why a cell that never stops dividing is a problem for the cells around her.
items.a: Her daughters keep dividing too and make a growing cluster. The cluster crowds the cells next to it and takes their space and food. A healthy body needs cells to divide only when it needs them.
items.why: A strong answer says that the cell makes more cells that crowd the others, and that a healthy body divides cells only when they are needed.

items.p: Cells from Henrietta Lacks were taken in 1951 without her knowing. They have helped to make medicines for 70 years. What should happen when something useful is taken from someone without asking?

views.says: These cells helped make vaccines and treat illnesses. The benefit to millions of people is huge.

views.who: A member of the Lacks family (an imagined view)
views.says: Nobody asked her or told us. The cells were part of her. People should decide what happens to cells from their own bodies.

views.who: A hospital ethics teacher (an imagined view)
views.says: Both things matter. Today researchers must ask permission, and the rules changed partly because of cases like hers.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? What would be fair to her family?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer weighs the benefit to many people against the choice of the person, and says what would be fair, such as asking first and sharing the credit.
items.why: This question has no single right answer. A strong answer shows that the child can hold two things at once, the good that came from the cells and the wrong of not asking.

items.p: Which statement about 'all your cells are replaced every seven years' is best?
opts: Different cells last very different times, so there is no one number
It is exactly right for every part of the body
It is right only for children
items.why: Gut cells last days, skin cells weeks, red blood cells months, and many nerve cells and lens cells a lifetime. So no single number fits the whole body.

items.p: Draw a timeline from a fertilised egg to a child. Mark where cells divide and where they take on different jobs.
items.a: A timeline starting with one cell, then 2, 4 and 8 cells, then a ball of cells, then shapes for skin, muscle and nerve cells, ending with a child. Arrows or labels mark division and different jobs.
items.why: A strong drawing shows division first, giving more and more cells, followed by cells taking different shapes and jobs.

items.p: Just after copying, a human cell has 46 chromosomes, each joined to an identical copy. How many chromosomes are there in all, and how many will each of the two daughter cells get?
items.a: 92 in all, and 46 for each daughter
items.why: 46 chromosomes plus 46 copies make 92. They are shared equally between two cells. 92 divided by 2 is 46.

quiz.p: Which sentence best describes cell division?
opts: One cell copies her instructions and splits into two
A cell grows bigger until she bursts
Two cells join to make one
quiz.why: Cell division is one cell becoming two. She first copies all her DNA, and then each daughter cell gets a full set.

quiz.p: What is copied before a cell divides?
opts: Her DNA, wound up in chromosomes
Her cell skin only
Her water
quiz.why: The DNA holds the instructions. If it were not copied, one daughter would get nothing.

quiz.p: Put these in order: pull apart, copy, pinch in two, line up.
quiz.why: The copying comes first, then the line-up, then the pulling. The pinching comes last.

quiz.p: A root with the tip cut off does not grow much. Which is the best explanation?
opts: Cells dividing at the tip make the new length
Roots grow from the seed only
The scissors made the root dry
quiz.why: Cells divide in a small zone at the very tip. Without the tip, there is nowhere for new cells to be made.

quiz.p: Which statement is true about the first cell of a new person?
opts: She divides again and again, and her daughters take on different jobs
She turns into a baby without dividing
She holds a tiny baby inside
quiz.why: A fertilised egg divides into 2, 4, 8 and more cells. The cells then take on different jobs.

quiz.p: A muscle cell and a skin cell in the same person differ because...
opts: They use different pages of the same instructions
They have different DNA
One of them is not alive
quiz.why: Nearly every cell holds the same full set of instructions. Signals from the cells around her decide which pages a cell uses.

quiz.p: Which part of a grown person has cells that are replaced after only a few days?
opts: The lining of the gut
Heart muscle
The centre of the eye lens
quiz.why: The gut lining is replaced in a few days. Heart muscle and lens cells last far longer.

quiz.p: Why are the cells of skin and the gut lining replaced often?
opts: They meet the outside world and get worn down
They are not alive
They are made of a different kind of DNA
quiz.why: Food and rubbing wear these cells. The body keeps making new ones to take their place.

quiz.p: A bacterium divides in two every 20 minutes. Start with 1. How many are there after 1 hour?
quiz.why: One hour is three periods of 20 minutes. The number doubles three times: 2, 4, 8.

quiz.p: About how many doublings of one cell would it take to reach about 35 trillion cells?
opts: About 45
About 350
About 35 trillion
quiz.why: Each doubling multiplies the number by 2. Ten doublings give about a thousand, twenty about a million, and forty-five about 35 trillion.

quiz.p: All the cells in your body are replaced every seven years.
quiz.why: False. Different cells last very different times. Gut cells last days, but many nerve cells in the thinking part of the brain last a whole life.

quiz.p: A ship has every plank replaced over many years. Some say it is the same ship, and others say it is a new one. What does this puzzle have to do with your body?
opts: Your cells are also replaced, so we can ask what stays the same
It shows that people never change
It shows that ships are alive
quiz.why: Many of your cells are replaced over time, as the planks are. The puzzle asks what makes something the same thing when its parts change, and there are different answers.

open_questions.q: How does a cell know when a gap has been filled, and when to stop dividing?
open_questions.why_open: Cells use many signals from their neighbours, and scientists understand some but not all. Cancer is partly a failure of these signals.

open_questions.q: Can adults make new nerve cells in the memory area of the brain?
open_questions.why_open: Two groups studied human brains in 2018 and found different answers. The brains were prepared in different ways, and the question is not settled.

open_questions.q: Why can a salamander regrow a leg, or a hydra regrow most of her body, when a human cannot?
open_questions.why_open: Humans have many of the same genes. Scientists do not yet know why the regrowing is switched off, or whether it could be switched on.

open_questions.q: Does the shortening of telomeres cause ageing, or is it only one sign of it?
open_questions.why_open: Cells with short telomeres stop dividing, but many things change as a body ages. Studies in people and animals have given mixed results.

open_questions.q: How does a fertilised egg 'decide' which of her daughters will become skin, muscle or nerve?
open_questions.why_open: Signals between cells are known in some animals, but the whole pattern in a human embryo is not yet understood.

open_questions.q: Why do some animals, such as some tortoises and a few sharks, seem to age so slowly?
open_questions.why_open: Their cells divide, repair and die like ours, but scientists do not yet know what protects them.
