maths.problem: You fold a sheet of paper in half again and again, and count the boxes after each fold. You get 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 and 64. How many boxes would there be after 8 folds, if you could fold that far?
maths.explain: The number doubles with every fold. After 6 folds there are 64. After 7 folds there are 128, and after 8 folds there are 256.
maths.context: In Fold and Count, you fold paper in half and count the boxes, as a cell divides into two.
maths.why_maths: Seeing the doubling pattern lets you work out how many cells there are after many divisions, without counting each one.

maths.problem: A fertilised egg divides, and each daughter divides, again and again. After 12 doublings, how many cells are there? Then say how many there would be if the egg had started with 3 cells.
maths.answer: 4,096 cells, and 12,288 if you start with 3.
maths.explain: 1 cell doubled 12 times gives 4,096 cells. With 3 cells at the start, the number is 3 times as big. 3 times 4,096 is 12,288.
maths.context: In Fold and Count, you found that doubling grows very fast. Here you look at it for a bigger number of divisions.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying a starting number by the doubling total tells you how many cells you will have, and shows how a small difference at the start becomes a large one later.

maths.problem: In the Cut the Tip test, the four roots on plate A grew 12, 18, 15 and 15 millimetres in two days. The four roots on plate B grew 2, 4, 3 and 3 millimetres. Find the average growth on each plate, and say how many times bigger the average on plate A is.
maths.answer: Plate A averaged 15 millimetres and plate B averaged 3 millimetres. A is 5 times as much.
maths.explain: A: 12 + 18 + 15 + 15 = 60, and 60 divided by 4 is 15. B: 2 + 4 + 3 + 3 = 12, and 12 divided by 4 is 3. 15 divided by 3 is 5. So plate A grew 5 times as much.
maths.context: In Cut the Tip, you measure four roots on each plate. Here are some made-up results.
maths.why_maths: An average shows what a group of roots did, so a single odd root cannot mislead you, and a ratio shows how big the difference is.

maths.problem: In Dots on a Root, five gaps start at 2 millimetres each. After a day, the gaps are 5, 3, 2, 2 and 2 millimetres, counting from the tip. What fraction of the total growth came from the gap nearest the tip?
maths.answer: 3 out of 4, which is three quarters.
maths.explain: The gaps grew by 3, 1, 0, 0 and 0 millimetres, which is 4 millimetres in all. The first gap grew 3 of those 4 millimetres. So three quarters of the growth was at the first gap.
maths.context: In Dots on a Root, you measure the gaps between dots after a day. Here are some made-up results.
maths.why_maths: A fraction of the total shows where most of the growing happens, which is more useful than a list of changes.

maths.problem: Marrow makes about 2 million red blood cells every second. About how many is that in one minute, and in one hour?
maths.answer: 120 million in a minute, and 7,200 million (7.2 billion) in an hour.
maths.explain: 2 million times 60 seconds is 120 million. 120 million times 60 minutes is 7,200 million, which is 7.2 billion.
maths.context: In the Replacement Race, you learned how fast your body makes new blood cells.
maths.why_maths: Big numbers are easier to understand when you multiply step by step, and they show how busy a body is, even when you are sitting still.

maths.problem: The lining of the gut is replaced about every 4 days. About how many times does it get replaced in a year, and about how many times in your life so far if you are 9?
maths.answer: About 90 times a year, and about 800 times by age 9.
maths.explain: 365 divided by 4 is about 91, so about 90 times in a year. 9 times 90 is 810, so about 800 times. These are rough, because the time varies.
maths.context: In the Replacement Race, you learned how often the gut lining is replaced.
maths.why_maths: A rough estimate is the right tool when real numbers vary, and it gives a sense of how often your body rebuilds itself.

maths.problem: In Pinch the Tulsi, stem A (pinched) grew from 12 centimetres to 14 centimetres and grew 4 side shoots. Stem B (not pinched) grew from 12 centimetres to 20 centimetres and grew no side shoots. How much more did stem B grow than stem A, and how many more side shoots does stem A have?
maths.answer: Stem B grew 6 centimetres more, and stem A has 4 more side shoots.
maths.explain: Stem A grew 14 minus 12, which is 2 centimetres. Stem B grew 20 minus 12, which is 8 centimetres. 8 minus 2 is 6. Stem A has 4 side shoots and stem B has none, so stem A has 4 more.
maths.context: In Pinch the Tulsi, you measure two stems. Here are some made-up results.
maths.why_maths: Subtracting the start from the end tells you how much each stem grew, so you can compare them fairly.

maths.problem: A dog has 78 chromosomes, a human has 46, a rice plant has 24 and a fruit fly has 8. Put them in order from fewest to most. How many more chromosomes does the dog have than the rice plant? Does a bigger number mean a cleverer animal?
maths.answer: Fruit fly 8, rice 24, human 46, dog 78. The dog has 54 more than rice. No, the number does not show how clever or how big a living being is.
maths.explain: Ordering the numbers: 8, 24, 46, 78. 78 minus 24 is 54. The number of chromosomes is just a count of how the DNA is packaged, and it does not say anything about how clever or big a living being is.
maths.context: In Paper Chromosomes, you saw that cells share chromosomes between two daughter cells. Different living beings have different numbers.
maths.why_maths: Ordering and subtracting numbers helps you compare, and reminds you to check whether a bigger number really means more.

how_we_found_out.story: For about thirty years, textbooks said that a human cell has 48 chromosomes. An American scientist, Theophilus Painter, counted 48 in the 1920s, and everyone trusted him. Counting is hard, because the chromosomes of a dividing cell lie piled on top of one another like a tangle of thread. In 1952, in Texas, a scientist named T. C. Hsu found that dividing cells soaked in weak salt water swell up, and their chromosomes spread out. The story goes that this began as a mistake in the lab. In 1955, in Sweden, Joe Hin Tjio, who was born in Java, tried this with Albert Levan on cells from human embryos. The chromosomes lay apart and could be counted clearly. There were 46, not 48. Other labs soon counted 46 as well.
how_we_found_out.who: Joe Hin Tjio and Albert Levan in Sweden, using a method found by T. C. Hsu
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: For about thirty years scientists believed that humans have 48 chromosomes. Better preparation of the cells, so that the chromosomes spread apart, showed that the real number is 46.
